What if you had to ride a Thwump sideways to get to another area? If the ghost doesn't trigger the Thwump it'd step on a mine or keep running into a wall or whatnot. If the Thwump recognizes the ghost as another ninja to annihilate, the timing could screw up the actual player.

If you wanted the ghost to just simulate movement so that (regarding the above scenario) it looks like it's riding an invisible Thwump, the game would have to be reprogrammed to record an entirely different type of demo data, aside from the current, even if the ghost-run is only for one play.

Plus, throw lag in there, player confusion, and all the other lesser points thrown in that I missed.

In short, it won't happen. I easily can see why anyone would want ghost movement, but it would be impossible to work in a game like N. Sorry.

Quote: Keron Cyst, 2006-04-19T17:45:54Z
Ghosts are all very fine, but how would they work? Racing games just have static terrain. N has action-performing objects.

What if you had to ride a Thwump sideways to get to another area? If the ghost doesn't trigger the Thwump it'd step on a mine or keep running into a wall or whatnot. If the Thwump recognizes the ghost as another ninja to annihilate, the timing could screw up the actual player.

If you wanted the ghost to just simulate movement so that (regarding the above scenario) it looks like it's riding an invisible Thwump (or if an invisible Thwump and other such objects were there to match the ghost), the game would have to be reprogrammed to record an entirely different type of demo data, aside from the current, even if the ghost-run is only for one play.

Plus, throw lag in there, player confusion, and all the other lesser points thrown in that I missed.

In short, it won't happen. I easily can see why anyone would want ghost movement, but it would be impossible to work in a game like N. Sorry.
Text added. This was my counter to another person who suggested ghost runs (which really aren't a bad idea in themselvesthey'd actually be pretty cool IMO, but given the way N was programmed, don't count on it).

Here we goooo!~ While there's a battle on the logic of Christianity in that other thread, I'll launch attacks on Evolution myself here.

1 just poses an example; I can't quite realize its core, but it more or less covers the point at hand, I think and/or hope. If someone can come up with a better scenario, feel free.



[ 1: guilt ]

Let's say you cheated on a test at skool, and no one in the entire classroom noticedthe person whose answers you discreetly observed, the teacher, everyone around you, etc. Why do you feel guilty of it? (Granted, some people actually are so embedded in sin that they don't feel guilt, but there's a first for everything. ) You got away with it; there's no possible way of being caught (in this particular scenario, at least), but you'reif you're the average personguilty of cheating. Whyzat?

[ 2: evol. of minor parts ] (probably the strongest of the 3 here)

This was actually the subject of my first main evolutionistic debate here; no one could refute it fully as far back as I can recall, but the info I provided was kinda ambiguous and quite uncommon knowledge, so I'll try to take a different, more "average" approach (that is, everyone should be able to understand this) and see if any new counters have come up since.

So let's say a year or three have passed and Spore comes out, and you develop a creature in Spore that looks like a Hetero sapiens, and then you just let auto-evolve take care of the rest, and you let it sit for a billion years or so while you work more in-depth on your ber-1337, aquatic Atlantis species. You then come back and observe the humanoid; it now sports hands which each have three fingers and a thumb.

Evolution dictates that if it isn't useful, it shall be thrown out. You let it auto-evolve and it becomes more human-like with every passing millennia, but its hands always have three fingers and a thumb, because if Evolution has it attempt to grow a stub of a finger (as it cannot grow a whole finger at onceexcept perhaps by a very drastic and incredibly precise mutation, since evolution is gradual), the stub will eventually be shown to be useless and future generations of the humanoid will lack it. Why do we have 5 fingers, then?

AND...

for those who say "Well, how do you know the humanoid's genus didn't form multiple species and one had four and the other had five?" Well, would five fingers really be that much more beneficial except in piano? (No offense to that! Piano pwnz; I just can't think of anything else right now since it's 1.14am) I don't think a species can defeat an entire other of its same genus just from the advantage of one finger. I guess you would have one point going if you claimed that a meteor or something wiped off the entire four-fingered humanoid species off the planet, but surely such an adaptive species would have spread to many parts of the globe by then.

Even if you smacked all of this about with a large trout, how would you show how any fingers evolved at all? Stubs can barely grip crap, you know (and the very original ones would have to be miniscule compared to stubs since the process is so gradual)

[ 3: efficient deathout-of-the-box concept ]

Evolution pertains only to bettering a species for survival, correct? No creature alive knows what death is like (for death is death, of course ). Thus, how would its cells not know what is beyond death? Physically, cells which are dead exert no energy, so why would not all cells "curiously" die (I'm not sure if that's the correct term) and achieve this state of energyless pureness?*

... And then you say "You don't know that the cells that survived and evolved over millennia into us today were more selfish than those philosophical counterparts. " Methinks that defeats #3, but I didn't consider individual cells to possibly have stuff other than instinct until just now, and I thought this was a cool concept anyways so I'm posting it.



* - sorry about that. That para was very, very poorly worded, so I wouldn't blame you if you misunderstood that. I can't seem to put into words my thoughts on the subject.

#9703 1 2006-06-26T05:39:12Z Keron Cyst
The Cold Within

Six humans trapped by happenstance
In black and bitter cold.
Each one possessed a stick of wood
Or so the story's told.

Their dying fire in need of logs
The first man held his back.
For on the faces around the fire
He noticed one was black.

The next man, looking cross the way,
Saw one not of his church.
And couldn't bring himself to give
The fire his stick of birch.

The third one sat in tattered clothes
He gave his coat a hitch.
Why should his log be put to use
To warm the idly rich?

The rich man just sat back and thought
Of the wealth he had in store,
And how to keep what he had earned
From the lazy, shiftless poor.

The black man's face bespoke revenge
As the fire passed from sight,
For all he saw in his stick of wood
Was a chance to spite the white.

The last man of this forlorn group
Did nought except for gain;
Giving only to those who gave
Was how he played the game.

Their logs held tight in death's still hands
Was proof of human sin.
They didn't die from the cold outside
They died from the cold within.

Darn Capitolist (the last guy of the 6).

Quote: Moridin
Suicide is not a state of mind that someone has because they are too weak and can't handle normal life. It is a psychological disease. Furthermore, it is not a cry for help. Suicidal people have a mental illness and it is not a conscious choise like "Oh, I have no money, and now I'm going to take my own life". Don't ever think that! Suicidal people don't want to have happiness, they don't care about happiness. They just want the pain to stop.

When questioned heavily (by more than one person) about why he thinks it is a disease, he countered with:

Quote: Moridin
http://www.metanoia.org/suicide/
http://www.save.org/basics/qna.html
http://preventsuicidenow.com/suicide-faqs.html
http://preventsuicidenow.com/bipolar-disor...nd-suicide.html
http://preventsuicidenow.com/schizophrenia-and-suicide.html
[...]

Futhermore, most people define mental illness as "BIG" things Multiple Personality Disorder, Alzheimer's etc. but there is so much more. Everytime you are not 100% allright and it is not due to anything physical, it is mental.

You need to separate people who "once-in-their-life" thought about suicide and those people how are and have gotten seriously and metally ill from rape, murder, divorse, violence, Bipolar Disorder, PTSD etc.

Quote: Code Hunter
there have been times when I thought of it, albeit breifly, but I very quickly realised 2 things.
1. I would never have the guts, because at the moment it sets in that it's final, forever. That leaves you no options, and the process of suicidal thought is that you beleive your out of options, so making that final is not a solution and you quickly see how backward or rather, pointless suicide is.
2. I know, even in the deepest depresssion that my love for my children is greater than my pain. I could never inflict the pain im in on my chioldren by leaving them, inexplicably fatherless. My kids worship their daddy, I make their life, they need me. I simply wont do it.

Quote

Quote

Quote
It's LAZY! "Oh, this is too hard... lemme give up."

... I think the sad truth is that some people here are just too dull to embrace any comical changes that happen to the forum. The... extremists... against this... really annoyed me how something so innocent and so harmless, with the sole intent of making people laugh or at least smile at this quirky spectacle can be hated with such a passion.... Well, see, the thing about that is that many changes to this forum have been decided by the people in public T&I polls. While the commoners (excuse the possibly interpreted-as-a-derogatory term) don't run the place, they sure have been major deciding factors of feature modifications to this board (such as my recent poll-only in T&I) and do deserve some sort of relative position in events that happen here. After all, this semi-democratic experiment of a forum seems to me to have flourished well during its time in its own way.

The Kablizzy Fiasco and all the other pranks I initiated in this place's past never regarded any alteration as humongous as a banner change; indeed, they were all just threads, but this sort of optional ability to pitch in or just ignore a simple thread drew people into it. This banner, however, shows up on every single page and in a way forces EVERYONE into it whether they like it or not, and this caused outrage, but even a bit more than I predicted in the beginning of the parade.

I was reluctant when I first saw the banner about the public's opinion but I decided to take the benefit of the doubt and initiate an equally humorous Pony Resistance; some who joined it took the Resistance seriously as a threat to the sane stability of the forums (unfortunately, they didn't realize that the Resistance wasn't half as serious as they thought It was just to open up the possibility of fun-n-games contests and the like). Q: Metanet's working on another game?!
A: Yep. Popularly dubbed TNG ("The Next Game"), people have been ranting over it for months now, even though it won't be released most likely until late 2008, because N+ has taken longer then expected. For up to date news, check the new blog: metablog.

Q: What will it have?
A: As it seems, it will involve nothing but robots (including the protagonist), a projectile weapon for the protagonist (in layman's terminology, a gun), and even more extensive depth in physicsin fact, supposedly most navigation throughout a level will occur through rope-swinging or a similar method. It'll also have a level editor, as always.

Q: What is it being coded in?
A: OpenGL and C++.

Q: Sweet!
A: Oh, and it'll co$t.

Q: What?! / Yes, a chance to contribute to such a great company!!
A: Of course! It has already been declared long ago that Metanet's games will be alternating from freeware to shareware to freeware; N is their first game and it's free, so Robotology will be shareware, their next game afterwards will be free, etc. Nothing's stopping you from donating as it currently is, tho'...

Quote: "-Slayer-"
http://wii.ign.com/articles/732/732982p1.html
Wii Titles will be Region-Free Region-Encoded
Games and online content will be region-specific.
by Alex Simmons

UK, September 15, 2006 - Wii games will not be region-free according to Nintendo UK's General Manager David Yarnton. Speaking exclusively with IGN at Nintendo's European Wii press event in London, Yarnton confirmed that Wii games and online content will be region-encoded, meaning European gamers won't be able to play titles from the US and Japan and vice-versa.

The news follows contradictory comments made by Perrin Kaplan, Nintendo of America's Vice President of Marketing and Affairs, which IGN reported on yesterday.


http://wii.ign.com/articles/732/732754p1.html
Nintendo Bundles Wiimote
My First Wii to ship with extra controller.
by Anoop Gantayat

September 14, 2006 - So you have your Wii, and you want to give everyone a chance to play, but you don't want to invest in a second controller? Nintendo has the solution for you!

In Japan, Nintendo will be bundling a Wiimote with Hajimete no Wii, a mini-game collection whose name we like to translate as "My First Wii." The game and Wiimote will be bundled together for 4800 yen, making it cheaper than a standard 5800 yen Wii game.

As detailed in an earlier article, Hajimete no Wii, a launch title set for Japanese release on 12/2, includes a variety of mini games designed to make players familiar with the Wii remote control. Included are pinball, table hockey and pool. The simple point-and-click shooting game Nintendo demoed at E3 is also included in this collection, as is a mini game where you move your Mii (the Wii name for your avatar) around on a city block.

This is the first Wii game to be bundled with a peripheral of any form. Nintendo is expected to bundle special expansion units with future titles depending on the requirements of the game.

 
http://wii.ign.com/articles/732/732802p1.html
Nintendo's Virtual Console Partners
Who's making games for Nintendo's retro service?
by Anoop Gantayat

September 14, 2006 - It seems as if everyone is making games for Nintendo's Virtual Console service. Well, everyone that counts, at least.

At the Japanese version of its Wii press conference, held yesterday in Tokyo, Nintendo announced 24 partner companies from whom we can expect games to appear on the retro games service.

The list of companies looks a little something like this:

# D4E
# Atlus
# Bandai Namco Games
# Banpresto
# Capcom
# Chun Soft
# Enterbrain
# HAL Laboratory Inc.
# Hudson
# Irem
# Jaleco
# Kemco
# Koei
# Konami
# Masaya
# Net Farm
# PAON
# Rocket company
# Sega
# Taito
# Takara Tomy
# Tecmo
# Sunsoft
# Square Enix

As noted in our earlier story, Nintendo has set up the following pricing scheme for Virtual Console titles in Japan. Famicom games will cost in the 500 yen range. Super Famicom games will go for around 800 yen. Nintendo 64 games will cost around 1000 yen. These are just approximate values, so it's possible that you'll be paying more for some titles.

Virtual Console games are purchased via Wii Points that are stored on your Wii system. Wii Points themselves can be purchased using prepaid cards or credit card.

Prepaid cards will be available in 1,000 yen, 3,000 yen and 5,000 yen varieties, but the 5,000 yen version is sure to get the most attention. Nintendo Japan will be included the Classic Controller with a limited number of 5,000 yen cards. This is normally a 1,800 yen device.

A new member has joined the Virtual Console family. In addition to the NES, SNES, N64, Genesis and Turbo Grafx, the system will also see titles for the MSX arcade system. At the press conference, Nintendo president Satoru Iwata expressed the desire to make the service compatibles with even more systems in the future.

Nintendo plans on having 60 Virtual Console titles available to Japanese Wii owners by the end of the year, breaking down to 30 from Nintendo platforms and 30 from the other platforms. Starting next year, the company hopes to release 10 new titles every month. It's unclear if this latter number is an internal target for Nintendo itself, or if it includes titles from third parties.

As Iwata has previously hinted, we can look forward to more than just classic games on the Virtual Console. Like Microsoft's Xbox Live Arcade service, Nintendo hopes to get original download content onto the Virtual Console. Some of the studios listed above aren't known for their retro game catalogues, hinting that work may already be on the way.

 
http://wii.ign.com/articles/732/732730p1.html
Wii DVD playback out!
NOA confirms that Wii will not play Hollywood DVD movies.
by Matt Casamassina

September 14, 2006 - Nintendo of America's vice president of marketing and corporate affairs, Perrin Kaplan, confirmed to IGN Wii today that its forthcoming Wii console will not play Hollywood DVD movies. The decision to remove the functionality was made in order to deliver the machine at a cheaper cost and because most people today already own DVD players.

More as it develops.
 
http://wii.ign.com/articles/732/732745p1.html
Wii channel breakdown
Details on the Wii user interface.
by Anoop Gantayat

September 14, 2006 - So what do you see when you turn on your Wii? The answer is Wii Channel, a browsing screen that gives you a full view of games and content accessible from your system.

Wii Channel was created with the idea of "expanding the number of television channels" available to users. In all, your Wii can have a total of 48 channels. By increasing the software stored within the system, you get access to new channels, all selectable from a main selection screen.

The main channel interface
An example of a channel is the Disk Drive Channel, which shows what's currently in the Wii disk drive, be it a Wii game or a GameCube game. You'll also find a picture channel, which gives you access to the pictures located on your system, and a news channel, which uses the internet to access the latest news. To purchase Virtual Console titles, you access the Wii Shopping Channel.

Disk Drive Channel
Go here to start up Wii and GameCube games.

Picture Channel
Access the pictures that are stored away on your SD Memory Card. The Wiimote is used to shrink and enarge pictures by moving the controller away and towards the screen. You also have access to image modification tools including paint brushes and paint buckets, and can view your images as a slide show.

Internet Channel
Go here to access the Opera internet browser. In addition to supporting flash (making this a step up from the DS browser), the browser uses the Wiimote to zoom in and out. The browser will normally cost money, but Nintendo will make it available for free download until June of 2006.

Weather Channel
This free weather service requires an internet connection. In addition to daily weather based on region, you also have access to a weekly forecast. The service gives you a view of the Earth, which you can rotate to access different regions.

News Channel
The latest news is automatically updated and viewable through this free service, which also requires an internet connection. The new channel is said to have "functions indicative of a game machine." Users can also change the font size for easy viewing.

Avatar Channel
In this channel, you create your own avatar, which is referred to as a "Mii." Your Mii is used in Wii games (as in Wii Sports) and can be transferred to your Wiimote and used on other Wii consoles. Nintendo chief software producer Shigeru Miyamoto commented at Nintendo's Japanese Wii press conference that this is a feature he's always wanted to have.

You'll also find channels for launching Virtual Console aps on the Famicom, Super Famicom and Nintendo 64. The interface also seems to allow players to assign shortcuts to Virtual Console titles, although it's unclear how Nintendo will be organizing all the games players will potentially have stored on their SD cards. Players will be able to view available software in various ways, selecting to view all Super Famicom games, for instance, or all games in the Mario series.

In addition to the individual channels, the Wii Channel interface gives you access to a message board, used for exchanging messages with your family members. Nintendo considers this similar to posting a memo on a refrigerator. In addition to writing text, you can also include images from your SD card in the body of messages. The message board service also gives access to the internet via WiConnect24, allowing those with whom you've exchanged friend codes to see your memos.

Out of my psych. textbook:

Quote: David Myers' AP Psychology
1. Authoritarian parents impose rules and expect obedience: "Don't interrupt." "Don't leave your room a mess." "Don't stay out late or you'll be grounded." "Why? Because I said so."

2. Authoritative parents are both demanding and responsive. They exert control not only by setting rules and consistently enforcing them but also by explaining the reasons, and, especially with older children, encouraging open discussion when making the rules.

3. Permissive parents submit to their children's desires, make few demands, and use little punishment.

4. Rejecting-neglecting parents are disengaged. They expect little and invest little.
If you don't already know, mine are authoritarian, sadly. The book says authoritative is the most efficient form of parenting.

Are there other forms? And how do your parents deal with you?

#262494 33 2006-12-01T05:24:27Z Keron Cyst
=====

The Snowball Fighter, by the Fluidmechanics Laboratory





The Game
You are a rubber duck. Believe it or not, you're a freakin' yellow duck which squeaks upon taking damage. Your tasks are many. They can range from defeating other ducks by throwing snowballs at them to solving puzzles in order to recapture treasure on high pillars, snatching away the love of a girl-duck, or any combination of these tasks combined... possibly under a time limit. You are The Snowball Fighter.



Yep, that's some treasure right there, and also shows the field; The Snowball Fighter always takes place in a square playing field. Maps are tiled, but movement is super-smooth and awesome. All the game has are the arrow keys to move, and Space Bar to throw a snowball. There is a key (I think V or B; it's been months since I played the game itself) are some optional alternate camera views to take advantage of the 3D (an overview and first-person view), but naturally the tilted diagonal angle is the best.

Aside from the primary objectives mentioned above, you must also sometimes push blocks Sokoban-style to get out of cramped sections and/or to rest upon blue switches. There are also red switches which can be triggered by throwing snowballs onto them, but the pillars they lower or raise revert to their original positions after a short time.

There are also small power-ups in various missions throughout the game. These can range to health boosts if you've taken a lot of damage, to temporary abilities (such as super-enlarged snowballs, which are actually required for some levels), etc.

Graphics & Sound
The graphics in The Snowball Fighter are incredible, especially for being a freeware game, but the real love lies in the sound. The innocent cries of enemy ducks taking damage or dying are freakishly cute, and the music is very grabbing, ambient yet bold in its composition, and fitting perfectly to the mood of the mission objectives at hand.

But the graphics are not to be ignored, either; the ducks' shadows are generated in real time as they rest on snow or blocks, or even other ducks. And don't forget the creation of those shadows (if they show very darkly in the first place, for there are also evening and night missions); surrounding the playfield is a wonderful random background, which only enhances the grandeur of The Snowball Fighter.



Playabity
The game is extremely simple and will get you addicted in no time. All there is to it is the arrow keys for movement and the Space Bar for your action. Aside from moving your own duck, you may also have to push blocks (simply by pushing against them with the arrow keys) - the camera assumes a straight top-down view if your camera is in the default position. The opposition in beginning levels may seem a tad simple, but just wait 'til you reach the meatier chunks near the middle and the end of the game, where the AI becomes extremely competent.

Physics
The physics in this game are stunning. Although there is no crazy ragdoll action like N, snowballs and your 3D depth-perception of them play a major role in attaining particular heights from climbing pillars in order to hit an otherwise unreachable switch. Many levels take advantage of the game's physics in combination with the sometimes obscure camera angle to formulate their puzzles. The snow on the "battlefield" even crushes as ducks navigate across them, and your duck slows in movement as it pushes blocks. This Lab has really done its research.



Verdict
The game is freakishly smooth, something that almost all games nowadays lack, and provides kiddy-level, totally blood-free violence great for all members of the family interested in working their brains in solving puzzles or raising a bit of adrenaline in tackling enemies. Unfortunately the game lacks a map editor, but the 25+ missions are more than enough to keep casual gamers busy. The graphics and sound are also extremely well-done and more than sufficeheck, morons nowadays try to release their crap as commercial when brilliant, underground coders like these guys publicize their work free of charge. Get it now. This game definitely lives up to its creators' name and indeed sports quite fluid mechanics. 98/100 (for lack of map editor, and relatively low repeating of game overall ;p Although it is nice to play again after a few months, once you forget all the tricks and turns, heheh).

=====

#13063 1 2006-12-22T06:18:46Z Keron Cyst
RAY-HOUND



RAY-HOUND's got to be the craziest, uh... mouse game I've ever played. If it could get its own subcategory in the field of shoot-em-ups, I'd call it a "Magnet Shooter."



Basically, the premise is this; you control a pacifist hovercraft in a playing field composed of vector-drawn hexagons. Stationary enemies spawn in each level and fire the popular siphon-like lasers we all know from many Japanese shoot-em-ups at you. Your craft has no weapons, but can manipulate any lasers that come into your control field.



Use the mouse to navigate the hovercraft. Left-click to activate the field and steal any lasers inside; they are now harmless and can pass through your hovercraft safely. Keep holding left-click and steer the lasers back at enemies. Click again to activate more fields; whenever you let go, any lasers under your command stray off in their regular direction.

Hint: If you jerk the mouse quickly so that your hovercraft temporarily emblazens into a blue triangle, you can use this effect so that if you have lasers under your command, you can use this technique to quickly siphon lasers in a particular direction instead of having them slowly follow a circular pattern.



The game is based on time. Every laser your hovercraft is damaged by takes 10 seconds off the clock. Gain more time by beating levels faster, by destroying enemy hovercraft. According to the website (and Google Translator, heheh), so far the game is just in early stages, levels are infinite, and enemies spawn in random parts of the field.


Hikoza's Products:

#277419 4 2006-12-26T17:54:07Z Keron Cyst
Well, I thought it was pretty interesting, and other Soldat players might like to check it out (although the two definitely can't be compared, heh; a programmer at the Soldat forums checked out the sourceit's open-sourceand concluded that it's basically a bunch of if-then statements).

Basically, you control a janitor from Goodco. Dog Food by the name of Joseph who has an umbrella, and is sent off to chase a bunny which escaped from the factory, presumably who was to be made into dog food.

Joseph can jump and walljump two or the same wall, not unlike N, and can pull out the umbrella for a slow drift, or to bat on the ground to solve various puzzles. The janitor can't attack enemies, but can try to lead them into lava pits, etc. or just directly avoid or run away from them.

The puzzles are pretty unique although not too complex. Some of the more action-filled levels are quite fun, and there's even a bit of stealth in the game as you try to get around very Predator-like aliens (we all know Marcinkowski's tangent for Predator ) called Zorths in later levels.

The graphics were all created in Paint, I think. Pretty cool stuff Also decent sound and music. The levels are nice, but the real fun lies in the craziness of the plot, and weird cutscenes.


Yes, there is a minimap. Holding it will allow you to look around your surroundings (the janitor in the above pic. is below the screen; that's a Zorth).



It's a very inefficient memory hog, tho'. Try closing unnecessary background programs before running; it's been known to crash a comp. or two at the Soldat forums.

#291576 36 2007-01-30T01:18:46Z Keron Cyst
I think having proto-N being able to actually recognize enemies and dodge them would be extremely difficult to program; take a generic FPS for example, which themselves are quite complicated: if it's low-quality the enemies won't even defend themselves and will try to simply rush you, and if it's a better FPS they'll simply take cover. Proto-N would have to not only be told to jump over an incoming Zap Drone or Floorguard, but also how high in case there is a ceiling of mines. What if there were two incoming Zap Drones with chase algorithms, one behind the other? How early should proto-N jump if there is a strip of one-ways above pointing up which leads to Thwumps or Chaingun Drones in another narrow alley just above it?

Proto-N would also have to be programmed to manage BounceBlocks, and I think its required use of them would take forever to code if it was to utilize them in such a way as to complete my No Grip for YOU, Young Ninja!. Same with momentum-ganing of climbing ramps.

In short, I'm not criticizing this idea; I think it is possible to make proto-N, but it'd take forever, and M&R probably don't have the time for it as I presume they'd move on to bigger and better things
#291586 2 2007-01-30T01:30:00Z Keron Cyst
Hm. I played a demo of Chibi-robo at Target

It's pretty cool; you basically control a robot a little less than half a foot in height (hence "chibi") who performs tasks within a certain time limit throughout a house by cleaning up messes (with a toothbrush!), picking up trash (where the trashcan is its head, which pops up), and zapping equally robotic spidery... things (with some sort of laser gun). There are also other devices such as a head-propeller, I think, and your chibi-robo, who's also accompanied by another hovering, owl-like drone, is constantly using up its battery; even as you stand idly, and much more when you're running and performing actions, a number-laiden bar on the HUD slowly depletes. Your cord dangles loosely behind you as you run, and every now and then you have to hold it over your head and plug it into a wall socket or other such source of power to rejuvenate. You can stand on chairs, tables, pull out drawers from desks, etc.

I felt it would be nice for a rental but that the repetition of action would make it a bit boring after a while; I'm not quite surprised that it's no longer being produced

#14471 1 2007-03-17T02:01:57Z Keron Cyst
rs.

Quote: Excerpts from Chapter 15: Psychological Disorders of David G. Myers' Psychology: Fourth Edition
1.Anxiety is part of our everyday experience. Fortunately for most of us, our occasional uneasiness is not intense and persistent. If it becomes so, we may have one of the three important anxiety disorders: generalized anxiety disorder, in which a person feels inexplainably tense and uneasy; phobic disorder, in which a person feels irrationally afraid of a specific object or situation; and an obsessive-compulsive disorder, in which a person is troubled by repetitive thoughts or actions. The symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder are commonplace, but their persistence is not. The sufferers are continually tense and jittery, worried about bad things that might happen, and experience all the symptoms of autonomic nervous system arousal. The tension and apprehension may leak out through furrowed brows, twitching eyelids, or fidgeting. In 1 of 75 people, for no apparent reason the anxiety may at times suddenly escalate into a terrifying panic attacka minutes-long episode of intense fear that something horrible is about to happen to them. Heart palpitations, shortness of breath, choking sensations, trembling, or dizziness typically accompany the panic. The experience is unpredictable and so frightening that the sufferer often comes to fear the fear itself and to avoid situations where panic has struck. Phobic anxiety focuses on some specific object, activity, or situation. Phobiasirrational fearsare a common psychological disorder that people often accept and live with. Some phobic disorders are incapacitating, however. Sometimes it is possible to avoid the fear-arousing stimulus, but with other phobias, avoiding fear-arousing situations may dictate never leaving home. Compared with the other disorders discussed in this chapter, phobias have an earlier onset, often by the early teens. As with the generalized anxiety and phobic disorders, we can we can see aspects of ourselves in the obsessive-compulsive disorder. We may at times be obsessed with senseless or offensive thoughts that will not go away. Obsessive thoughts and compulsive behaviors cross the fine line between normality and disorder when they become so persistent that they interfere with the way we live or when they cause distress. At some time during their lives, often during their late teens or twenties, 2 to 3 percent cross that line from normal preoccupations and fussiness to debilitating disorder. The thoughts become so haunting, the rituals so senselessly time-consuming that effective functioning becomes impossible.

#321259 8 2007-05-15T00:10:56Z Keron Cyst
You can't use mathematics with infinity. A graph is the only way to work TRULY infinite #s; everything else rounds off. Now that I realize, you're right about the graph needing to be concave But there's still a gap nonetheless.

If you want a verbal explanation, here's a brilliant one:

Quote
There's no way to make use of an infinitely accurate infinitely repeating number, for several reasons.
First, there's no way to BE infinitely accurate.
Second, there's no way to handle infinite numbers, except by placeholders.
Third, it's totally useless to have actually infinite numbers, and use them as such, for the above reasons.

So a compromise is reached by rounding the numbers off at a sufficiently high digit. This way, normal algebra rules can still apply, and a useful number can be found.

[...] while that one [here, nevermore's post] seems to favor being proof, you can never actually complete the [math]. So, what's the square root of pi? It's impossible to determine, so we approximate to whatever decimal point of accuracy we need.

Besides. For all the limit-at-infinity (or at zero resulting in infinity), you're using a different set of rules than standard algebra. And any decent math teacher will tell you that it isn't actually real numbers you're finding, you're just finding what they APPROACH WITHOUT EVER REACHING. So .333... isn't actually equal to 1/3, it's just infinitely close (which, for basically all forms of math, is close enough to say it is the same). Due to that, by saying 1/3 = .333..., you're assuming what you're trying to prove is correct, which is a fundamental flaw in trying to prove something like this.

I originally was going to send this to Pavel Vyacheslav in response to musical taste, but it was too large an IM for AIM to accept. So I thought I'd put it here, in the B&T, so I can get a lot of unreasonable flames.

- - -

Really... no offense, but ANYONE can compose that kind of stuff. It's horridly repetitive, and very simpleI mean, there is in nearly ALL cases only one melody for its listeners to follow. I'm not going to deny that a few pieces are very complicated and require extremely skillful guitar-players to pull off, but those are few and far between; I think it attracts crowds because it's loud & fast and many of the artists' facial and body makeup/clothing/mask is death-related, which we all love (N, Soldat, etc. :P).
Classical, on the other hand, is very complex, and is not noisy and repetitive all the time. You can listen to the same piece twice and (if you're paying close attention) hear a melody or harmony in another part of the music that you didn't catch the first time around; not so with rock, where there is one basic melody which can easily be followed along in most works. Classical's meditative. Honestly now, if you needed to concentrate on a mental task, would you listen to rock or classical? And if you somehow declare "Rock!", classical has been scientifically proven to assist with health and it rejuvenates the body, if you haven't heard of The Mozart Effect alreadythose who listen to the stuff after surgery ALWAYS recover at least a tiny bit faster on avg. than those who listen to nothing or something else. The Case for a Creator, Chapter 8: The Evidence of Biochemistry

... "Kenneth Miller of Brown University has another objection to your trap," I said. Then I read him Miller's comments:
            
            Take away two parts (the catch and the metal bar), and you
            may not have a moustrap but you do have a three-part
            machine that makes a fully functional tie clip or paper clip. Take
            away the spring, and you have a two-part key chain. The catch
            of some mousetraps could be used as a fishhook, and the
            wooden base as a paperweight; useful applications of other
            parts include everything from toothpicks to nutcrackers and
            clipboard holders. The point, which science has long understood,
            is that bits and pieces of supposedly irreducibly complex
            machines may have differentbut still usefulfunctions.(7)

            "That's a strong point," I said. "Maybe an irreducibly complex system could develop gradually over time, because each of its components could have another function that natural selection would preserve on the way toward developing a more complex machine." 
            "That's an interesting argument," he said.
            I leaned forward. "Doesn't this dismantle your case?" I asked.
            Behe didn't flinch. "The problem," he replied," is that it's not an argument against anything I've ever said. In my book, I explicitly point out that some of the components of biochemical machines can have other functions. But the issue remainscan you use numerous, slight, successive modifications to get from those other functions to where we are?
            "Some of this objection seems a bit silly. Could a component of a mousetrap function as a paperweight? Well, what do you need to be a paperweight? You need mass. You need to exisyt. An elephant, or my computer, or a stick could be a paperweight. But suppose you go buy a paperweight. What would it look like? Most of them are nondescript, roundish things. None of them look anything like a precursor to a mousetrap. Besides, look at what he's doing: he's starting from the finished productthe mousetrapand disassembling it and moving a few things around to use them for other purposes. Again, that's intelligent design!
            "The question for evolution is not whether you can take a mousetrap and use its parts for something else; it's whether you can start with something else and make it into a mousetrap. The problem for evolutionists is to start with a less complex system and build a more complex system. Even if every component could theoretically have a useful function prior to its assembly into the mousetrap, you'd still have the problem of how the mousetrap becomes assembled."
            "Explain further," I said.
            "When people put together a mousetrap, they have the disassembled components in different drawers or something, and they grab one from each drawer and put it together. But in the cell, there's nobody there to do that.
            "In molecular machines, components have portions of their shape that are complementary to each other, so they connect with each other in the right way. A positive charge can attract a negative charge, and an oily region can attract another oily region. So if we use the mousetrap as an analogy, one end of the spring would have to have a certain shape or magnetism that just happened to attract and fit with another component of the trap. They'd all have to fit together that way until you had the whole trap assembled by itself.
            "In other words, if you just had the components themselves without the ability to bring the other pieces into position, you'd be far from having a functioning mousetrap. Nobody ever addresses this problem in the evolutionary literature. If you do any calculations about how likely this could occur by itself, you find it's very improbable. Even with small machines, you wouldn't expect them to self-assemble during the entire lifetime of the earth. That's a severe problem that evolutionists don't like to address."

#333025 3 2007-06-19T15:01:48Z Keron Cyst
Well, one of my most important (not the most, as I can't think of what my most pressing concern is right now) suggestions is that letter grades should be removeda 69.5% is not the same as a 79.4%. One of my friends (we're talking high school here) always tries to do his best throughout the entire year solely so he can sleep and not care during the finals in the last weeks of school. This is pretty idiotic in my opinionin universities, the last test tends to count for over 50% of the end grade, so my friend and others like him aren't getting final-exam practice, and letter grades also make people lower their goals. For example, in my AP Physics C class, I had a 71%, a strong C (more lenient curve; the lowest possible B- in specifically that class alone is a 74.5%), and my final exam was 200/200 possible pts.; even if I got everything perfect I could not possibly have picked up to a 74.5%, so I simply aimed to fail the test, quite literally (get around 50-60, which is what I successfully did), only to prevent myself from falling into a D. If letter grades were removed, I would instead strive to do my best on everything no matter what (although I honestly don't think I could've gotten much farther than what I -did- receive on that test... flippin' hard, man, that!).

So, As, Bs, Cs, Ds, Fs... all should be removed, and everything should be %-based. The system is dumb as it is with letter-grades; those who get a 79.5% will be placed with people whose average is ~85%, and thus be even more unprepared for the ensuing class for being lucky, and vice-versa for those who score an 89.4% but barely fail to get an A.

What problems are there in the college/university system? I'm not really too sure of their structure since I've yet to be exposed to any as a student.

Faade is an artificial intelligence-based art/research experiment in electronic narrative  an attempt to move beyond traditional branching or hyper-linked narrative to create a fully-realized, one-act interactive drama. Integrating an interdisciplinary set of artistic practices and artificial intelligence technologies, we have completed a five year collaboration to engineer a novel architecture for supporting emotional, interactive character behavior and drama-managed plot. Within this architecture we have built a dramatically interesting, real-time 3D virtual world inhabited by computer-controlled characters, in which the player experiences a story from a first-person perspective. Faade was publicly released as a freeware download / cd-rom in July 2005. 

You, the player, using your own name and gender, play the character of a longtime friend of Grace and Trip, an attractive and materially successful couple in their early thirties. During an evening get-together at their apartment that quickly turns ugly, you become entangled in the high-conflict dissolution of Grace and Trips marriage. No one is safe as the accusations fly, sides are taken and irreversible decisions are forced to be made. By the end of this intense one-act play you will have changed the course of Grace and Trips lives  motivating you to re-play the drama to find out how your interaction could make things turn out differently the next time.

Everything that has ever had a beginning has always had a cause. God never "began" to existHis current existence needs no cause. As Obby noted, it isn't difficult to exist for ever if there is no time to keep track of such existence.

I've felt quite many times that I even did not want to return to the board ever again; of course, this would have been contradictory since I must out of responsibility, so I even sometimes concocted a mental fantasy of creating an alternate account who I would play right alongside the disgraced Cyst, and rise up in public opinion over a course of several months or more of activity, and eventually retake over as a new user.

The only other accounts I have ever made here were out of paranoia and board security, and have 0 total posts. Otherwise, I have always come back quietly, marred, but with the humble thoughts of renewing myself. And amidst all of the grotesque humiliation, people see through my frank posts who I am, or what I am like, and slowly learn to overlook my uglier aspects, or learn why and understand them.

If you don't let others get to know you by establishing a strong name for yourself (whether it begins positively or negatively), and you just back out while it still overwhelms you at the moment and you end up forever pretending to be another person who must create his own foundation from scratch instead of simply rebuilding from ruined (but at least existent!) concrete, you will never get far in creating lasting bonds or forming lasting respect from others.

Man, all these aliases vex me insanely... I myself have more justification to settle upon a new account than anyone else, yet I'm still here after possibly one or two almost sleepless nights from humiliation, and here are all these other members who have embarrassed themselves less than I have of myself, who try to conceal their inevitable faults under a username-veil instead of manning up and facing them with ground teeth.

So man up and stay. If you can't overcome your own problems on a computer messageboard, nobody will.

Quote: blue_tetris, 2007-12-04T12:20:02Z
A movie about a process doesn't necessarily address its origins. You can talk about the development of architectural designs and how one leads to the next, without extensively talking about why cavemen picked up rocks and put them on other rocks.
True, but methinks architecture is not nearly as complicated as the origin of life! One could go so far as to state that one can't compare anything to it because it's so unique. But yeah, I concede anyways, so I'll state now that the below has nothing to do with the movie (in that regard) and attacks the atheistic (or "nontheistic," whatever the term is) stance on naturalistic origination.

As for the formations, there indeed are plenty of natural self-ordering tendencies, such as the popular NaCl. But amino acids demonstrate only slight affinities, and:
Quote: Stephen C. Meyer in Lee Strobel's "The Case for a Creator"
"First, you need the right bonds between the amino acids. Second, amino acids come in right-handed and left-handed versions, and you've got to get only left-handed ones. Third, the amino acids must link up in a specified sequence.... Run the odds of these things falling into place on their own and you find that the probabilities of forming a rather short functional protein at random would be one chance in a hundred thousand trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion trillion. That's a ten with 125 zeroes after it!

"And that would be only one protein moleculea minimally complex cell would need between three hundred and five hundred protein molecules. Plus, all of this would have to be accomplished in a mere 100 million years, which is the approximate window of time between the Earth cooling and the first microfossils we've found."

Furthermore: How could you get a line of amino acids and then proteins to all come together in some coincidental spot to then combine into a functional cell? They would form crystals over and over again regardless of available time rather than form cells, and chemically declare "hahahahahahaha" in ordered but repetitive mantra instead of a genetic message. You need to have irregular sequencing for information, but even then it would only make "Ball the threw he"the correct information for communication (in language as well as DNA, which hardens this analogy that much more) would be "He threw the ball," whose complex grammar & syntax cannot be achieved through naturalistic processes.

#403973 24 2008-01-25T06:15:02Z Keron Cyst
I just saw it today. Kind of surprised me, this thread already appearing

It was very... unique; I'll tell that much. Basically, to sum, think of an American, more alien-like Godzilla in New York with a monstrous twist (heh, and that one addition by its writers is probably the scariest feature of the movie)... with the ENTIRE movie being shown from the perspective of a camcorder, from the point-of-view of generic civilians caught in the event of the creature's uprising. It was really interesting! I was warned beforehand by one of the people in my group who went to watch it that quite some people who saw it earlier had to leave because of motion-sickness, but none of the people in my theater showing were affected.

It's rather unrealistic, even ignoring the presence of the super monster, but I enjoyed it better than the Tom Cruise version of War of the Worlds. (The computer graphics were brilliant, perhaps only topped by few movies other than even Superman Returns, in my opinion.) Actually, I'll tell this much: if you thought War of the Worlds sucked, but thought that a different director, perhaps producer, and actor(s) could have turned it around into an amazing movie, you'll probably like Cloverfield, since to me it was like an excellent remake vaguely resembling WotW's style, in a sense. The post-apocalyptic/horror atmosphere was superbly developed in an exponentially better way than WotW, although I found the ending to be rather abrupt... too abrupt, IMO. The entire plot is a little like Cave Story in that you might feel like piecing together events afterwards, to comprehend it better, which is perhaps what Dave was referring to. It would be best enjoyed with a small group of friends who were terrified by Aliens or other movies of that nature (unfortunately, the supernatural doesn't faze me, so I personally didn't get the best effect, ha). Perhaps Resident Evil fans might like it even.

I thought Beth's lover (one of the chars.) was Tom Cruise at first, but the credits showed him to be a "Stahlwart-David" or something like that (don't exactly remember). He looked (and even acted) very similarly like Cruise. All of the actors/actresses were great. Expect a lot of "sh--" and "Oh, ---"... naturally.

BTW, just reiterating:
Quote: Sniperwhere, 2008-01-23T16:36:04Z
And no, it's not like Godzilla in any way(except for being a monster in a city).
And, one of the friends in my group afterwards said that the directors (or whoever) said that everything could be explained in
Spoiler: the most improbable ways... (seriously don't click this if you plan to watch it; this reveals basically everything).the monster was awakened from the deeps of the ocean from contact by a deep-sea oil rig, and was able to endure the numerous RPGs and even the B-2 stealth bomber's bombing run because it had been lying dormant for millenniums and was supporting all the land and sea above it, so its carapace had become super-hardened and powerful.

But even then, why it had minions (and their own strange [stupid, even?] random WotW-style effects on humans), why it paused before chomping up Han at the end after so much unhesitant terror, and how the civilians survived the helicopter crash completely unscathed (and the camera, too, haha... 'til the very end!) were all totally ridiculous, though; the chopper should've exploded into a blazing fireball upon ground impact! Supposedly the camera was fully charged at the beginning of the monster's siege upon Manhattan, so theoretically it could have lasted all the way 'til day at the end of Cloverfield, since it was paused several times, and for several hours following the helicopter fall.

Han's successful recording of their ascension of the blasted skyscraper is also beyond me, since one would [most likely... haha [ts:smiley=19]] need both hands to grab the pipes and scale the fallen structure, and it can be clearly inferred that the camera was hand-held, not shoulder-mounted or anything.

Trained military soldiers do not charge a gigantic monster blindly spraying at it like Soldat n00bs. That was so dumb. They should have coordinated and taken cover behind cars and buildings and stuff... not just running right at it firing randomly in its general direction! Ha. [/]

But if you can suspend your disbelief, it's a great work, albeit short (methinks even less than 90 minutes). I told you it ended abruptly... I give it somewhere between 7.5 & 8 (naturally out of 10); I'm a harsh critic, so that's very decenta.k.a. probably not worth watching in the theater, but if you don't watch Cloverfield in particular in a theater, you lose some of the rumble effect of the movie since it's especially horror-based at times. You'd definitely want to rent it on DVD at least, if you're into post-apocalyptic, futuristic, chaos/war, suspense/horror/thrill, action... etc.

#18960 1 2008-01-25T18:05:33Z Keron Cyst
Thanks to some supreme introspection and others' excellent help, I think I see why I can't relate to others; I tend to close everything off to myself. I also tend to ridiculously overthink what to say at times, so much so that I'm usually almost completely silent with groups, as small as they may be, of people who I don't know very well. In contrast, regardless of how well I know him/her, I can hold excellent talk with just one other. For some reason, I can only talk absolutely comfortably with others if I know them extremely well, or if I've known them from the past (it may seem odd at first, but just having ice broken by simply knowing each other's names in elementary school, or something, and meeting each other years later is amazingly powerful).

I think that's why I'm so fascinated by the Internet; one can simply revise what one has to say through post-editing (I think I edit nearly every medium-sized post afterwards at least once), and can take as long as one needs to construct a response. Even in IMs, there is still a psychological barrier that helps (at least me) in conversing, but in a real-time, real-presence conversation, rapid-fire talk pressuring you to respond immediately basically disables me if the talk doesn't absolutely require me to reply (again, as in with groups, which I would otherwise like to be more a part of); I either speak uncertainly, or the subject moves right before I have been able to craft a strong or interesting response.

Hnw can I make myself more assertive ("more confident"?), or more of an expressive "speak-as-it-comes-to-mind" kind of guy? I wonder how many others feel like this.

There IS no steady rock to stand on, no music to force everyone's attention on, no lasting focus; it's all sand falling through the fingers. The topic can just sway wherever it wants, and can at times quickly to nothing at all (that is, "awkward silences" and that sort of junk). Its fluctuation messes me up so much I basically am like a mentally handicapped moron, just observing everyone else apathetically, if I'm not directly involved in the conversation; and, if someone DOES specifically direct it to me and say "So Josh, what did you think of... [it]?" if I don't have an extremely solid stance on it, I hesitate idiotically before and while responding, as much as I don't like to or want to.

For example, this is primarily why I didn't buy a ticket for my school's midwinter dance, which is occurring today, and which is why I've never been involved in any such events (co$t also factors in, heh).

YES.

(I mean, to what T3chno posted above. )

Don't make the same mistakes we did! Join clubs as SOON as possible and as much as possible. Try to become presidents of activities and stuff (be shameless in what you do, perhaps). Be known in the school. Join student council. For example (I don't know if you're a super-overachiever like the rest of the people I tend to mingle with or not), all the Ivy League universities' applicants already have straight-As, 2100+ on their SATs, etc. and there is no distinguishment academy-wise. Be the first white dude to lead Asian Student Union, as one of my friends just achieved this year, or something. START a club on your own, in fact, as one of my friends did three years ago (the Middle Eastern Club; incidentally, he's Syrian). THAT's the stuff people look for.

Or volunteer. Accumulate hundreds of hours of community service after school and/or on the weekends at a hospital or something. I stupidly did that only during one summer, filing, typing, sorting away like a drone, and achieved a mere 126 hrs. Community service & extracurricular activities are number 1.5 on your to-succeed-in list. (Marching band is required? That's really interesting...)

You're really smart to ask this. Get all the stuff out of an old senior like me, ha.

The lit. books are fine. Difficult stuff like Homer's The Odyssey can be adapted to once you force yourself through the first four chapters or so; by then you basically mold to the writer's style, and they become easier to read. Summer reading is simple; a chapter or three a day suffices, with a notebook next to you to track neat quotes. Some of the books may be boring, but some of them are nice choices and you may become interested on your own in your reading.

I too took nothing but Honors or AP courses for literature. We seem to go through somewhat less than ~7 novels every year, 2 or 3 being instantly covered via summer reading, from what I can recall. It's not that much, considering the months.

Yo puedo hablar espaol un poco. I took three years. The textbooks are very... well, academic-feeling. It's pretty much memorization, although some words and sentence formats interlace through the languages. I'm not sure of what "advice" I can give in particular on that, than simply reviewing vocabulary and grammatical concepts every other night. If all else fails (usually it did in the case of my classmates and I), learning fell to raw memorization of the stuff. But languages are big in today's world; if you feel you can really make something practical out of it, by all means pursue it.

Health and P.E. are required (for me, P.E. goes only to sophomore year... heh). In health (which I took over the summer with a friend right before we incame as freshmen), we just learned about drugs and stuff. High school P.E. (well, mine anyways) is rather similar to middle school P.E.



Put simply, I found high school to be like this, in comparison to middle school: MS teachers are aware that you have others who give you homework, so you don't have very much. But HS teachers are tougher, in fact a bit more like elementary school, simply concentrated to their particular field (of lit., history, science, math, foreign lang.... a little less: drama, music, electives - computer courses, ceramics, etc.). And to eat up your remaining time, you've got plenty of clubs & other activities, which almost always meet weekly during lunch, to check out; Interact and Key Club (community service clubs) in particular come to mind. You'll want to head for those two first.

#415536 43 2008-03-10T06:06:05Z Keron Cyst
Okay, my auditions are done. I want to summarize all of my experiences, just for my own notes, and for anyone half-interested in the process of music auditions. I'll detail the cities that the schools were in, because I've been told by several that major factors aside from the quality of the school and the teacher to be taught by are friends, perhaps weather, and city life.



Feb. 16 (15? don't remember):
Boston, MA - The coldest of all the four cities I visited. I walked by the Church of Scientology as I went to dine with a relative of a church friend of my parents'; her perspective was a very, very nice revelation of what the city life is like (a.k.a. excellent!): Because it is so cold (even when I arrived, I saw traces of ice from leftover snow some days before), people flock indoors to spend their free time doing little other than shopping and dining, and hanging out at pubs, like P.F. Chang's Bar & Bistro or The Cheesecake Factory, so a social life is totally robust here. The mall that she took me to was superb (though the Legal Sea Foods restaurant we ate at was an atrocious rip-off of crap "food" pretending to be in a high-class restaurant; I still remember my ~$20 seafood casserole's virtual 'puddle of garlic' with a few random shrimps, scallops, etc. tossed & melted inside Though their starting bread as well as famous New England Clam Chowder were indeed top-notch). Boston had a mind-blowing, sophisticated subway system; all of the cities did (except Philadelphia's, which I didn't experience, and only might shortly after this post, but probably not).

The New England Conservatory - audition was okay. Like Curtis, I messed up in the Liszt; this was the first, so I was still getting used to the audition process, so I didn't anticipate the cut that one of the four judges had me execute, which wrecked my confidence for pretty much the rest of the way, and provoked me to concentrate more on avoiding wrong notes than to focus on musical expression. I think I will get low scholarship... if I get accepted at all. I played (in this order) the Valle d'Obermann (I was cut from the beginning of the Henle-Urtext third page to the tremolo section, and then was stopped at the end of it), Bach's G-Major Prelude & Fugue from Book I (they cut me off before even the first page of the fugue), the exposition of the first movement of Beethoven's Waldstein Sonata (ugh, did horribly there), its the second movement (cut me RIGHT while I was about to enter the main right-hand melody), Debussy's Pour le Piano - III Toccata (that was good; they cut me off right before the development of the development, a bit after the middle. They listened to that and the Liszt the most, which were incidentally my best pieces), and Chopin's tude Op. 10 No. 8 (cut me right as I entered the minor part, after seemingly arguing over each other after the Debussy as to whether they should hear it at all).

The Bach was horrendous. I tell you, one of the most difficult composers, that guy... haha.

I won't mind if I don't get accepted, though; I did not like the school; this was on par with Curtis as probably the worst of the schools, or at least the schools' first looks, to me. The building was known to be the States' oldest conservatory (~150 years old ), and it seemed like the practice rooms for pianists were always limited, judging from the masters-degree-pursuing student who I stayed with, who did not really like NEC.; she said that even at 6am the practice rooms were always filled, and she even sometimes had to resort to practicing on an upright. The grands weren't that good either, in my own practicing before the audition (and after, for the Peabody audition to come later). The cafeteria food was junk. The new (this was her first year) admissions officer was quite fair.



Feb. 18:
Baltimore, MD - I didn't experience very much; I was only there for one day. But the weather was nice. It was warmer than Boston. The buildings were very rundown and boarded-up with wooden planks... vandalized... etc. But it was actually quite safe. This had the most African-Americans out of them all, kind of interestingly. The Light Rail was just as awesome as the Boston subway. OASIS, which is the name of the student body which volunteers to connect the rest of the students with Peabody's administration, said that the city is very safe, with volunteer police-style people, undercover cops, and more protection. There is a free shuttle which runs every half-hour from Peabody to Johns Hopkins. The students said that it is easy to find work because there are many churches and other places that are always in demand for musicians. The harbor was just some blocks away, and that sports plenty of attractions. It's a great place.

The Peabody Institute of the Johns Hopkins University - This was exponentially better. I especially liked how in the Valle d'Obermann the judges did not cut me directly to the tremolo section, but cut me earlier than the NEC faculty did at the beginning, instead to the C-Major sectionwhich I REALLY loved, since I can be very expressive in that passagewhich let me lead into the tremolo section (and yeah, they cut me after that like NEC did). Then they listened to my 1st Waldstein mvt. (almost if not completely all the way to the recapitulation, I think), and the 2nd mvt. (a bit into the melody, more than NEC), then the entire Chopin tude Op. 10 No. 8. I didn't do well there because I was concentrating on making the left hand (which carries the melody) sing, so much that I had quite some missing notes in the right hand, which was very, very bad. But I still think I did loads better than NEC. They did not hear the Bach (!) nor the Debussy (!) at all.



Mar. 6:
The Manhattan Borough of New York City, New York - The best!! Probably the best, anyways. I stayed with a church friend, which showed me just how cramped the expensive apartments can be, haha. Half the cars were taxis, and the SuperShuttle taking me from the airport to the apartment took nearly an hour longer than what was originally estimated. The $16-shuttle itself was generously paid for by a most kind businesswoman, who overheard the rather confusing directions that the information-booth lady at the airport suggested I take after I showed her the 'poor' HopStop.com directions I was originally planning to abide by.

I really liked the city. Now that I look at it, I experienced the least of Baltimore out of all the cities, because in all the others, I met one person who lived in the city who could enlighten me to the life; here, I met a friend of the friend who I was staying with, who told me about how action-packed NYC can be, and about the public transportation, while he drove to fetch his 11-year-old dog from a daycare center. I really liked how the blocks were organized; avenues increase in # going west (2nd Avenue, 3rd Avenue, etc.; the negative avenues have names), and streets increase in # going north (23rd Street, 24th Street, etc.). In contrast to the trains I rode during February, all the subways here were jam-packed; there were always, ALWAYS people standing, whereas in the others there was ample space to sit down. Figures.

I loved it, though. Saw policemen with bomb-sniffing dogs in the subways... saw a troop of 10 police officers patrolling the block between Penn Station and the United States Post Office (which had Corinthian-style columns from Roman times, just like AP Art History describes! Haha )...

The Manhattan School of Music - My best audition. Definitely my best audition. I will love to be accepted here, and if I'm accepted to Peabody I'm going to have a hard time deciding (unless one definitely gives a lot more scholarship than the other). I began with the Waldstein Sonata's 2nd mvt., then I was cut to the 3rd mvt. (unfortunately, the way I had written my repertoire on the paper to be handed to the judges, they seemed to perceive that I didn't have the first mvt. readyI wrote the times for only the last two mvts.4 & 9 min.which is probably what made them think that, but I'm more comfortable with the 3rd than the 1st mvt. anyways). Then...

And this was EXCELLENT...

The judge announcing the cuts said, "Please play the Bach fugue." Just the fugue! So I played the fugue through (even more surprisingly, the entire piece), and the prelude not at allthat was wicked. I think my bringing-out the multiple voices impressed them the most (which is why they require all pianists to play a Bach fugue... you hear a simple melody, and then it manifests itself among 2-5 different voices throughout the piece, shifting from the right hand to the left hand and sometimes even both simultaneously, and you have to manage your fingers very, very intricately to successfully bring it along with other secondary voices out to the audience). Then they had me end with the Debussy Toccata, cutting me surprisingly very close to the end, just two or three pgs. away (which later one of the judges personally commented on, saying that I played it ridiculously fast... though I did tell him that I was going by Walter Gieseking's recording). Even with the judge's (judges'? ) astonishment to the Toccata speed, this audition I still felt the most confident on. Incidentally, my teacher himself graduated from MSM. I think I will like the 24-hr. practice rooms here.

(I say that I did well with the Bach here as compared to NEC since I noticed more voices to bring out between February & March while I was analyzing it at home. I discovered many more hidden voices in the notes... really crazy, that Bach.)



Mar. 8:
Philadelphia, PA - not a good city. Well, the regions are vastly different (north & south are poor, slum-like, and dangerous; east & west are decent, more urban, and safer; the buildings all over are old, naturally). The place I stayed at was kind of in the middle of such areas. The weather was like Baltimore, perhaps a tad colder (though this could have been because it had rained for nearly the entire day of the audition). On the bus ride to Curtis I met a public high school geometry teacher who complained all the way to my stop since I met her at the bus waiting booth; of how bad the students are (I wasn't surprised at this ), of how bad the teachers can be (that was a bit interesting, how she for some reason lacked T.A.s and was forced to sharpen all of her own No. 2 pencils for a state test), of how poor the food was (related to the price) in comparison to Baltimore. She seemed to glorify Baltimore when I mentioned the other cities I'd been auditioning at, and kept repeating how excellent the doctors werenaturally, because of Johns Hopkins. My New York friend also said that Philadelphia was probably her least favorite, though a friend of hers who graduated from Penn University said he enjoyed downtown Philly. Hm...

The Curtis Institute of Music - I ph41l3d miz3r4bly. That was probably the worst audition I had (and at the most important school, too!), even worse than NEC. I messed up in the Valle d'Obermann - my hands were extremely sweaty (I stupidly did not wipe them against my pants right before playing or anything, for some reason), so my right hand slipped from a black key to a white key while carrying the melody in a slow section. Ouch. They listened then to the exposition of the 1st mvt. of the Beethoven, and then Chopin's tude Op. 10 No. 6, all the way through. By that time (esp. at the end), I completely lost my focus on musical expression and already (correctly) anticipated that I wouldn't make it to the final round, which will be hosted later today, the 10th, as I fly back home. A 14-year-old named Han Yin made it through.

Strangely enough, although Curtis is supposed to be the most important (as it is the one private music school in the entire States that provides free tuitionlittle wonder, with a $300 audition fee for each applicant! Sheesh ), Philadelphia did not appeal to me much. At all. What especially cushioned the blow of my audition was a fellow applicant from Boston, who apparently had played alongside my own audition at MSM just two days earlier. He told of how world-famous faculty (which Curtis had more of than any of the other schools) do not necessarily imply a more personal or smarter teacher, and may even be unreliable since they may be giving concerts often and not be available most of the time.

So we'll see. The results from the other schools will arrive by mail in early April. Ooh. For now, I must work on the Jose Iturbi Piano Competition... so many new pieces to learn (and old pieces to return to) for its roughly 3-hr. repertoire for its 4 stages (preliminary, semi-final, and final I & final II )... but first I must return home. Now I'll be waiting for a Liberty taxi to get me 6.7 miles to the airport for $26.25 at 4:30am...

Of course a .ZIP can get deleted regardless of whether it is passworded or not! It is just a file like any other. Extra drives (Removable Disk F:, G:, H:, etc.) come from all sorts of information-transferring hardware, mainly USB ports. You can attach a flash-drive to a USB port (a tiny multi-gigabyte memory stick) or the memory card from a digital camera into an MMC/SD slot (I don't know... that's a small hole that's in my HP Pavilion D4100E). You can attach an external hard drive to hold more stuff in case your internal (built-in, literally inside the motherboard... CPU!) hard drive is too full.

For example (I'm sure you know of this at least), CDs and DVDs create Removable Disks (sometimes commonly M: or N:) for as long as they are left inside their respective reader-writers.

Those Earth-exclusive probabilities look plausible, but you certainly can't generalize the universe to pop out Earth-perfect planets left & right. The M13 Cluster broadcast from some decades ago was pointless.

The solar system's Sun is in the top 1% as the heaviest in elements in the universe (galaxy, perhaps? I don't have any books with me at the moment... can't remember exactly), compared to the plethora of red dwarfs that abound throughout the galaxy yet fail to give heat. and the solar system itself shows just how important location is. Even a planet so revered as a terraforming subject as Mars, so close to Earth, failed to produce life (inarguably, complex or long-term at least). The solar system's other planets buffer Earth from innumerable asteroids; we know of the power of just a single large-enough asteroid, able to wipe out hundreds (thousands?) of species, maybe irreversibly wreck a planet's entire ecosystem in just some years, and of the presence of such rocks from mere count of craters on the moon and other planets.

Soooooo many more dangers abound; Earths cannot form in irregular and ellipsoidal galaxies because their solar systems would take them on fun cruises through gamma rays and other dangerous electromagnetic radiation, not mentioning steering rather perilously close to the black holes that hold their galaxies together in the center. Even the location of Earth inside the Orion Arm of the Milky Way is in the safest haven possible, guarded from the surrounding exploding supernovae in a ridiculously narrow field of survival.

I definitely didn't spend as much time right now as you did, but I'll see if I can return to this later. It's not that easy to make an Earth.

Faith and Deeds

14What good is it, my brothers, if a man claims to have faith but has no deeds? ... well, let me not respond immediately.
